title: 1950 Douglas C-54D disappearance
summary: A Douglas C-54 Skymaster with 44 people aboard disappeared en route from Anchorage, Alaska to Great Falls, Montana over remote Yukon Territory. Two hours after departure, the pilot reported the aircraft on schedule over Snag, Yukon with ice on the wings and no other issues. The aircraft never checked in at its second waypoint at Aishihik and was never heard from again. Despite a massive search effort involving 85 aircraft and 7,000 personnel covering 350,000 square miles of rugged terrain, no trace of the aircraft was ever found.

notes: Aircraft never found; cause entirely unknown; airframe icing and engine trouble reported; loss of control inferred from disappearance

title: Llandow air disaster

agencies.name: UK Ministry of Civil Aviation Court of Enquiry

summary: An Avro Tudor V chartered for a rugby tour approached runway 28 at abnormally low altitude. The pilot increased engine power to correct the descent, bringing the aircraft up steeply to 100 m with a nose-up attitude of 35 degrees, then the aircraft stalled. The right wingtip struck the ground first, followed by nose and left wing impact which separated from the fuselage. The investigation found the center of gravity had been moved significantly aft due to aircraft loading modifications, reducing elevator effectiveness.
probable_cause: Aircraft center of gravity moved aft of limits by improper loading modifications, reducing elevator control effectiveness and leading to stall on approach recovery attempt.

factors.evidence: the aircraft had been stripped to accommodate another six passengers beyond the original 72-passenger booking, and the probable cause was the loading of the aircraft, which had moved the centre of gravity considerably aft of where it should have been

title: 1950 Air France multiple Douglas DC-4 accidents
summary: Douglas DC-4 Ciel de Picardie crashed into the sea near Bahrain during approach on 12 June. The pilot-in-command failed to keep accurate altitude checks during a timed descent procedure. Two days later, a second DC-4 on the same route crashed at nearly the same location with similar circumstances, suggesting environmental or procedural factors contributed to both accidents.
probable_cause: The pilot-in-command did not keep an accurate check of his altitude and rate of descent during the timed approach procedure, thus allowing his aircraft to fly into the surface of the sea. Fatigue could not be ruled out.

factors.evidence: The aircraft overflew the airfield at about 1000 feet and crashed

events.text: At 20:42 the aircraft called Bahrain approach reporting at 6500 feet asking for clearance to descend.

At 21:15 the aircraft reported finals and the tower gave permission to land on Runway 29.
The aircraft was found in 12 ft of water 3.3 miles from the end of the runway.

notes: Two accidents in same event; recorded first crash of June 12

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 2501
summary: A DC-4 operating transcontinental service from New York to Seattle was over Lake Michigan at approximately 3,500 feet when the crew requested descent to 2,500 feet. Shortly after, radio contact was lost. Witnesses reported hearing engine sputtering and seeing a flash of light. The aircraft wreckage was never found despite extensive Navy and Coast Guard search operations. Some light debris and human remains were recovered from the lake surface.
probable_cause: The probable cause could not be determined as the aircraft wreckage was not located underwater. At the time of last contact, the aircraft was entering a squall line and experiencing turbulence.

title: 1950 Australian National Airways Douglas DC-4 crash
summary: The Amana departed Perth for Adelaide but crashed 22 minutes after takeoff while flying at unusually low altitude. Witnesses observed rough engine running and backfiring; engines periodically lost power completely. Investigation found significant corrosion product and water in the fuel system of at least two engines, which caused rough running and temporary loss of power from all engines.
probable_cause: Water in the fuel system caused corrosion and loss of power from all engines on at least one occasion during the climb.

title: TWA 903
summary: Flight 903 departed Cairo at 23:35 with 48 passengers and 7 crew for Rome in good weather. As the aircraft was climbing at 10,000 feet, the crew reported that the number three engine was on fire and requested priority return to Cairo. As the aircraft was returning to Cairo, the number three engine separated from the aircraft. The crew attempted a forced landing in the desert about 65 miles north-northwest of Cairo, killing all 55 occupants. Investigation determined the cause was failure of the rear master rod bearing on the number three engine due to sludge buildup in the crankpins blocking oil flow.
probable_cause: Failure of the rear master rod bearing on the number three engine. The failure caused the rear crankpin to overheat and fail, whereupon all the rear connecting rods failed, tearing through cylinder walls and crankcase. Sludge buildup in the crankpins blocking oil flow was thought to be the root cause.

factors.evidence: the crew reported that its number three engine was on fire

notes: Root cause clearly identified through investigation; resulted in improved oil screens and revised oil change intervals

title: 1950 Heathrow BEA Viking accident
summary: In visibility of 40 yards, the Vickers Viking was conducting a GCA approach to London Airport. After reaching decision height at 400 yards from the runway, the pilot announced he was overshooting. Seconds later the aircraft struck the runway, skidded 140 feet, then crashed. The inquiry could not establish precisely what happened, but likely the pilot descended below decision height to escape fog, only aborting when the aircraft broke below the clouds.
probable_cause: Probable intentional descent below decision height to visual reference in conditions significantly below minimum; pilot misread visibility information relayed by ATC.

title: Air India 245
summary: Air India Flight 245 crashed into Mont Blanc while descending toward Geneva Airport in stormy weather, killing all 48 aboard. The aircraft hit the Rocher de la Tournette mountainside at 4677 meters on the French side of Mont Blanc. The last transmission reported the crew vertical with Voiron at 4700 meters altitude. The stormy weather prevented immediate rescue efforts and no survivors were found.

title: 1950 Tête de l'Obiou C-54 crash
summary: A Douglas C-54B-1-DC en route from Rome to Paris crashed into the Grande Tête de l'Obiou mountain, killing all 58 occupants. The aircraft was 40 nautical miles east of its reported position at Istres, indicating navigation error. Night was falling and the mountain was enveloped by cloud at the time of impact.
